title: An autonomous, evolvable expanded genetic alphabet

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a living system that routinely stores, copies, reads, and evolves substantial genetic information using additional letters alongside the canonical DNA bases. Its defining advance would be integration: the organism would manufacture the necessary expanded-alphabet building blocks, maintain them across many functional genetic elements, retrieve the information they encode, and transmit useful changes through successive generations.

Here, autonomy means biosynthesis of the necessary expanded-alphabet components from specified ordinary nutrients. It does not mean independence from nutrition or a suitable environment. Evolvability means that heritable changes involving the additional letters can contribute to useful functional variation, while copying remains sufficiently faithful for the intended application. These are proposed properties of the integrated system, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

An expanded alphabet must be distinguished from an alternative alphabet. Thomas and colleagues’ ALIEN DNA uses four artificial bases in place of the canonical four and is isoinformational with ordinary four-letter DNA. It therefore explores different molecular chemistry without increasing alphabet size. Its sequencing demonstration is relevant to reading unfamiliar genetic letters, but it does not itself demonstrate the additional letters or autonomous living heredity envisioned here.

significance.text: If achieved, the integrated capability would establish a broader practical architecture for heredity: a living system could sustain and evolve functional information with more genetic letters than canonical DNA provides. Researchers could directly investigate how alphabet size, molecular recognition, copying fidelity, and information retrieval affect an evolving biological system. This is a conditional scientific impact judgment, not a prediction that the system is feasible or imminent.

Alternative genetic chemistry already supplies a rationale for these experiments. Thomas and colleagues argue that ALIEN DNA’s charged backbone and rule-based pairing provide properties relevant to Darwinian evolution. That argument helps motivate research on alternative informational polymers; it is not evidence that their sequencing system underwent organism-level evolution or that a larger alphabet will automatically improve biological performance.

As a downstream possibility, additional genetic letters could support new ways to encode biological functions, including routes to proteins containing noncanonical amino acids. Particular products, superior performance, compatibility across organisms, and reliable operation outside a controlled setting would each require further design and validation. More available letters do not by themselves establish more useful information, better organisms, or a complete replacement for existing biology.

missing_breakthrough.text: The candidate breakthrough is coordinated organism-level operation. As an engineering synthesis, the required capability joins component biosynthesis, sustained genetic maintenance, functional information retrieval, and evolution in one living system. The supplied evidence documents relevant components but does not establish either completion of this integration or its continued absence as of 1 November 2026.

A proposed biosynthetic barrier is making the required expanded-alphabet components from defined nutrient inputs at rates and concentrations compatible with growth and inheritance. A proposed maintenance barrier is preserving additional letters across diverse functional sequences and repeated cell divisions, rather than retaining only a small isolated construct. These requirements also entail demonstrating that the additional letters remain part of the inherited functional information instead of being lost or replaced.

Information retrieval remains a concrete enabling challenge. The Thomas paper identifies a need for routine, accurate sequencing that can accommodate unfamiliar base chemistry and alphabet sizes, and reports that its ALIEN workflow was not yet optimized for accuracy, throughput, sample size, or read length. Its reported sequencing accuracy is a measurement of a readout component, not an organism’s replication fidelity; the two must be assessed separately.

A further proposed barrier is balancing stable inheritance with useful variation. A convincing system would need to preserve established functions while allowing heritable changes involving the additional letters to generate selectable effects. Changes confined to canonical DNA, or adaptation achieved by eliminating dependence on the expanded alphabet, would not alone demonstrate the intended evolvability.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Zhang, Ptacin, Fischer and colleagues’ A semi-synthetic organism that stores and retrieves increased genetic information as a 29 November 2017 publication, DOI 10.1038/nature24659. It attributes to that study storage and retrieval using an unnatural base pair, incorporation of noncanonical amino acids into a protein, and import of required unnatural triphosphates from the medium. However, the retained PubMed material contains only a cookie challenge, so those details and the bibliographic identity cannot be independently confirmed from the supplied copy. The earlier statement that its abstract had been inspected is therefore not retained. This access limitation does not show that the reported historical findings are false. If the described import dependence is confirmed, it would distinguish that demonstration from the biosynthetic autonomy proposed here.

The inspected 2025 Thomas article provides secondary bibliographic support for earlier semisynthetic organisms with expanded genetic alphabets. This supports the background that expanded alphabets and organism-level experiments precede the present proposal, while leaving the specific findings of the inaccessible 2017 source unverified within this evidence set.

Thomas and colleagues’ Sequencing a DNA analog composed of artificial bases, published on 6 August 2025, DOI 10.1038/s41467-025-61991-9, reports de novo nanopore sequencing of contiguous artificial-base regions in synthetic oligonucleotides. Four testing strands contained 28-nucleotide ALIEN regions, with reported mean single-read per-base accuracy of 74 ± 1% (standard error of the mean). The reported evaluation includes edge exclusions described in the figure caption. The artificial regions were flanked by canonical-DNA adapters, so the complete experimental constructs were not composed exclusively of artificial bases.

That result establishes a sequencing component in an in vitro workflow. The methods describe externally prepared and handled synthetic oligonucleotides; use of E. coli to express experimental proteins elsewhere in the workflow does not turn the experiment into a living expanded-alphabet heredity system. The reported accuracy and limited sequence scope also do not establish reliable reading of extensive genetic programs, autonomous component synthesis, or evolution of functions dependent on additional letters.

The supplied review examined the Thomas main article text and PDF, but did not independently validate graphical evidence or linked supplements. A reporting-summary PDF yielded almost no extractable text. These limits constrain broader interpretation without negating the limited sequencing result supported by the main text. Separately, the supplied record contains no freshness assessment establishing the field’s status through 1 November 2026; the dated 2025 result should not be treated as a complete account of subsequent progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: construct a living system that biosynthesizes its necessary expanded-alphabet components from explicitly specified ordinary nutrients, and independently reproduce the result. Define the permitted nutrient inputs and environmental conditions so that autonomy has a testable meaning. Establish that continued operation does not depend on supplying the required expanded-alphabet components externally. These are proposed criteria, not a published consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible expanded-alphabet component biosynthesis from specified ordinary nutrients

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: maintain and use additional letters across a predefined number and diversity of functional genetic elements for a predefined propagation duration. Measure retention, copying fidelity, information retrieval, and the relevant functions throughout propagation. Set fidelity thresholds according to the intended application and distinguish biological copying errors from sequencing errors. Controls should test whether the functions actually depend on the expanded alphabet and whether loss or replacement of its letters explains apparent stability.
completion_criteria.label: Functional expanded-alphabet elements meet predefined propagation and fidelity requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: show useful, heritable changes involving the additional letters, connect those changes to measured functional effects, and reproduce the genotype–function relationship. Independent laboratories should be able to repeat the core construction, propagation, and functional results under disclosed conditions. The demonstrated range of sequences, functions, environments, and durations would define the result’s practical boundaries; finite tests could establish breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Useful heritable expanded-alphabet changes show reproducible genotype–function relationships

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with GEN-02, Design and construct complex eukaryotic genomes to specification, and GEN-03, Precise, programmable replacement of large genomic regions in existing cells: all concern engineering genetic material. GEN-02 emphasizes constructing complex genomes, GEN-03 emphasizes replacing substantial regions in existing cells, and GEN-09 emphasizes the molecular alphabet and its autonomous inheritance. Success in genome construction or replacement would not by itself establish expanded-alphabet operation; GEN-09 likewise does not require achievement of either broader capability.

Conceptual comparison with GEN-01, A predictive, causal map of the genome’s regulatory code, and GEN-11, Predicting genetic interactions across backgrounds and environments: these concern explaining and predicting how genetic information produces effects. An expanded alphabet could create additional questions about regulation and genetic interactions, but maintaining extra letters would not itself solve those predictive problems. Conversely, predictive models of canonical genomes would not demonstrate autonomous use of additional letters.

Conceptual comparison with GEN-10, A testable reconstruction of the origin and fixation of the genetic code: expanded-alphabet organisms could provide experimental systems for studying alternative relationships between inherited information and biological function. GEN-09 concerns constructing a working hereditary system; GEN-10 concerns explaining a historical origin and fixation process. A viable engineered alternative would demonstrate a possibility without establishing the route taken by early life.

Conceptual comparison with GEN-05, General laws of environmentally induced, sequence-independent inheritance; GEN-06, Transferable clonal seed reproduction across major crops; and GEN-07, Predictably controllable inheritance in wild populations: these share an interest in inheritance but address different mechanisms and scales. GEN-05 concerns inheritance independent of sequence changes, GEN-06 concerns reproductive transmission in crops, and GEN-07 concerns population-level inheritance control. GEN-09 concerns the sequence alphabet itself; its success would not establish any of those other capabilities.

Conceptual comparison with GEN-08, Reconstructing an organism’s cell divisions and histories from inherited molecular marks, and GEN-04, A retargetable delivery platform for genetic medicines across the body: additional letters might eventually support new molecular recording or therapeutic designs, but those are conditional applications. GEN-08 requires reliable historical reconstruction, while GEN-04 requires effective targeting and delivery across the body. Neither follows from expanded-alphabet heredity alone.

Beyond the roster, the concept overlaps with synthetic biology, nucleotide biosynthesis, molecular evolution, and sequencing. Thomas’s ALIEN system is a relevant alternative-alphabet approach: its four artificial bases and sequencing workflow help investigate unfamiliar informational chemistry, while remaining distinct from an expanded alphabet maintained and evolved autonomously by a living organism.

unresolved_issues: The 2017 source’s identity and attributed storage, retrieval, noncanonical-amino-acid incorporation, and triphosphate-import findings remain unverified from the retained cookie-challenge artifact.
Whether the integrated autonomous, evolvable expanded-alphabet capability remained unachieved as of 1 November 2026 is unresolved because no freshness assessment was supplied.
The supplied review did not independently validate graphical evidence or linked supplementary material for the 2025 paper; the reporting-summary extraction was nearly textless.
Specific nutrient inputs, alphabet chemistry, functional scale, propagation duration, and application-specific fidelity thresholds remain to be chosen for an executable completion test.
The feasibility of integrating biosynthesis, functional maintenance, information retrieval, and useful evolution in one organism is not established by the supplied component results.

brief.title: Life that makes and evolves extra genetic letters
possible: Researchers could grow living cells that make, copy and use extra DNA letters—the chemical units that carry genetic instructions—from ordinary nutrients. Those cells could pass useful changes involving the extra letters to their descendants.
The extra letters could offer new ways to encode biological functions, including proteins with unusual building blocks.
why: This would let researchers test how the size of a genetic alphabet affects inheritance and evolution in living cells. They could study how cells preserve unfamiliar instructions while allowing useful changes to arise.

sources.who: Yorke Zhang, Jerod L. Ptacin, Emil C. Fischer and colleagues
sources.showed: Engineered bacteria stored and read genetic instructions containing two extra DNA letters. They used those instructions to put unusual building blocks into a protein, while receiving the extra letters’ chemical components from their surroundings.
sources.quote: The resulting SSO both encodes and retrieves increased information
sources.cited_for: Living cells can store and use instructions involving extra genetic letters.
sources.not_established: The cells did not make the required extra-letter components from ordinary nutrients or demonstrate useful evolution involving those letters.

sources.showed: The team read synthetic DNA regions made from four artificial letters by measuring electrical signals as strands passed through a tiny pore. Ordinary DNA flanked those regions. This alphabet replaces the usual letters rather than adding to them.
sources.quote: Here we demonstrate de novo nanopore sequencing of DNA comprised entirely of the four anthropogenic DNA bases.
sources.cited_for: Unfamiliar genetic letters can be read directly from electrical signals.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate an expanded alphabet maintained and evolved by living cells.

shown: Zhang and colleagues demonstrated living bacteria that stored extra genetic letters and used them to make a protein with unusual building blocks. Their cells depended on externally supplied components for the extra letters.

Thomas and colleagues read short artificial-letter DNA regions outside living cells with about 74% accuracy per letter in a single reading. That measures the reading method, not how faithfully a cell copies its DNA.
missing: A living system must make its required extra-letter components from specified ordinary nutrients.
Cells must retain and use extra letters across varied functional genetic instructions over repeated generations.
Reliable reading must work alongside faithful copying, with errors in each measured separately.
Useful inherited changes must involve the extra letters, while established functions remain intact.

milestones.label: Cells make extra-letter components from ordinary nutrients
milestones.explanation: Cells would have to make the required components from defined ordinary nutrients, without external supplies of those components, with independent replication. This would establish self-supply under specified conditions.

milestones.label: Extra letters support lasting, reliably inherited functions
milestones.explanation: Varied functional genetic elements would have to meet preset standards for retention, copying, reading and function over a defined duration. This would establish dependable inheritance that requires the extra letters.

milestones.label: Inherited extra-letter changes produce reproducible useful effects
milestones.explanation: Useful inherited changes involving extra letters would have to cause measured functional effects, with independent laboratories repeating the core results. This would establish useful evolution involving the expanded alphabet.

uncertain: Can component production, faithful inheritance, reliable reading and useful evolution work together in one living system?
Which nutrients, functions, sequence diversity, propagation duration and error thresholds would define a convincing demonstration?

page.title: Autonomous evolution with an expanded genetic alphabet
page.definition: A living lineage copies and uses DNA containing additional bases alongside A, C, G and T, makes the extra bases’ nucleotide building blocks from specified ordinary nutrients, and undergoes selection on heritable changes involving those bases. Autonomy excludes feeding the extra bases or their nucleosides or nucleotides.

goal.need: The larger alphabet increases the possible triplets shown below. In 2017, two extra-letter codons directed protein synthesis using supplied nucleotides. The goal couples this coding capacity to inherited variation without supplied synthetic nucleotides. A separate readout experiment on 6 August 2025 achieved 74 ± 1% single-read accuracy (s.e.m.; four strands, 102 reads; central 24 of 28 artificial bases scored), using four replacement letters rather than an expanded alphabet.

figures.caption: Possible three-base sequences
figures.note: Calculated as the number of letters cubed. These are combinatorial counts, not numbers of experimentally assigned amino-acid codons.

statements.context: A milestone under unnatural nucleotide polymerization systems in the consortium’s engineering-biology roadmap.

statements.body: Foundation for Applied Molecular Evolution-led collaboration
statements.quote: One horizon in synthetic biology seeks alternative forms of DNA that store, transcribe, and support the evolution of biological information.
statements.context: The paper concerns artificially expanded genetic information systems, which add independently pairing nucleotides to the canonical alphabet.

completion.title: A living lineage biosynthesizes its expanded alphabet and evolves functions through its extra bases.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed demonstration in one living lineage shows DNA with more than four bases being copied, inherited and used for a measured function while all required extra-letter nucleotides are biosynthesized from a disclosed, defined nutrient medium containing none of the extra bases, their nucleosides or their nucleotides. Selection enriches a heritable functional improvement caused by a change involving an extra base; the evolved function still depends on extra letters. Nutrient inputs, propagation duration, retention and genotype–function evidence must be stated. No numerical fidelity, genome-size or generation minimum is established.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s integrated autonomy-and-evolution test was located.
completion.basis: Searches of EBRC’s roadmaps and assessment, developer papers, ISO standards, prize criteria and DARPA targets found no published integrated autonomy-and-evolution test. This criterion combines EBRC’s nucleotide-biosynthesis goal with the developers’ storage, transcription and evolution goal. It adds no unsupported genome-size, fidelity or generation cutoff.

milestones.title: DNA with extra letters is amplified by PCR while retaining its additional base pairs.
milestones.criterion: Peer-reviewed PCR copies an additional base pair alongside A–T and G–C, with retention measured after amplification. Hydrophobic pairing: Malyshev et al., published 6 July 2012, reported 87% to >99% retention after approximately 10^12-fold amplification; uncertainty used three sequencing reactions per primer. Hydrogen-bonded pairing: Kim et al., published 6 November 2025, reported >97% retention of modified Z:P pairs over 10,000-fold amplification. These measurements are not universal pass thresholds.
milestones.set_by: Expanded-alphabet research community; PCR-copying tests used by Malyshev et al. and Kim et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: Here, we examine the PCR amplification of DNA containing one or more d5SICS-dNaM pairs in a wide variety of sequence contexts.

milestones.title: Dividing cells inherit DNA with an additional base pair alongside the two canonical pairs.
milestones.criterion: Peer-reviewed propagation in dividing cells retains an additional base pair in recovered DNA. Hydrophobic pairing: Malyshev et al., published 7 May 2014, retained d5SICS–dNaM over about 24 doublings in 15 hours, estimating ≥99.4% retention per doubling; the time-course reported n = 3 and supplied 0.25 mM of each unnatural triphosphate. Zhang et al., published 23 January 2017, extended testing to repeated growth and additional sequence contexts using dNaM–dTPT3 and Cas9. No corresponding hydrogen-bonded cellular demonstration was located.
milestones.set_by: Expanded-alphabet research community; cellular replication and retention tests used by Malyshev et al. and Zhang et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: the endogenous replication machinery uses them to accurately replicate a plasmid containing d5SICS-dNaM.

milestones.title: Cells express a gene through an extra-letter codon and its matching transfer RNA.
milestones.criterion: Peer-reviewed cellular expression links extra-letter DNA to RNA and a measured gene product. Hydrophobic pairing: Zhang et al., published 29 November 2017, decoded AXC and GXC codons, where X denotes NaM, using cognate extra-letter transfer RNAs. Propargyl-lysine incorporation at position 151 of superfolder green fluorescent protein was 96.2 ± 0.3% and 97.5 ± 0.7%, respectively (95% confidence intervals; n = 4 separate colony-derived cultures). Unnatural triphosphates were supplied. No corresponding hydrogen-bonded cellular demonstration was located.
milestones.set_by: Expanded-alphabet research community; information-retrieval test demonstrated by Zhang et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: retrieval of the information requires in vivo transcription of the UBP into mRNA and tRNA

milestones.title: Selection yields extra-letter DNA whose measured function depends on its additional bases.
milestones.criterion: Peer-reviewed selection and amplification recover extra-letter DNA with a measured function. Hydrogen-bonded pairing: Sefah et al., published 30 December 2013, selected the GACTZP aptamer ZAP-2012, with a 30 nM dissociation constant for breast-cancer cells; replacing Z or P reduced binding. Hydrophobic pairing: Kimoto et al., published 7 April 2013, selected Ds-containing aptamers against two proteins, with dissociation constants of 0.65 pM and 0.038 nM. These were selections outside living cells; the opened abstracts give no independent-selection or binding-assay replicate counts.
milestones.set_by: Expanded-alphabet research community; selection, amplification and functional characterization used by Sefah et al. and Kimoto et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: The affinity is diminished or lost when Z or P (or both) is replaced by standard nucleotides

milestones.title: Living cells biosynthesize the non-natural bases of an expanded DNA alphabet.
milestones.criterion: Engineered pathways generate non-natural bases in living cells; EBRC gives no rate or concentration threshold. Hydrogen-bonded pairing: Zhao et al., version of record 22 September 2022, enzymatically converted deoxyxanthosine monophosphate to deoxyisoguanosine monophosphate outside cells. Li et al., published 25 May 2023, made expanded-alphabet triphosphates from supplied nucleosides using an in-vitro kinase pathway. These are component results. No complete cellular biosynthesis demonstration for either pairing chemistry was located.
milestones.set_by: Engineering Biology Research Consortium, 2019 roadmap, unnatural nucleotide polymerization systems.
milestones.threshold_quote: Engineered biosynthetic pathways capable of generating non-natural bases in vivo.

milestones.title: A living lineage supplies its extra nucleotides and maintains functional expanded-alphabet heredity.
milestones.criterion: In one living lineage, endogenous synthesis supplies the extra-letter nucleotides needed for DNA propagation and functional information retrieval during continued growth on disclosed defined nutrients, without feeding the extra bases, nucleosides or nucleotides. This combines the biosynthesis milestone with cellular inheritance and expression. EBRC and the developer papers provide no published integration threshold or propagation minimum. No demonstration meeting this conjunction was located for either pairing chemistry.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of EBRC’s roadmaps and developer papers found no separate test for integration of biosynthesis, inheritance and expression.

not_found: No outside completion criterion combining nucleotide biosynthesis, expanded-alphabet inheritance, functional expression and cellular adaptive evolution was located.
No numerical fidelity, propagation-duration or functional-scale standard for that integrated capability was located.
Full-text access to the Sefah selection, Kimoto selection and Li nucleotide-pathway papers was blocked; their abstracts were accessible.
The opened selection abstracts did not disclose independent-selection or binding-assay replicate counts.
